    Memory management

    Last updated on 2026-11-14 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 20 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How does R store objects in memory?
    • When does R copy an object?
    • Why is growing an object in a loop so slow?

    Objectives

    • Recognise when R will create a copy of an object
    • Explain why pre-allocating memory is more efficient than growing vectors and data frames
    • Determine when to cache variables

    Objects created in R are stored in memory (RAM). This makes them fast to access, but R slows down as the memory fills up, and creating objects also takes time. There are well-known pitfalls in R when it comes to managing memory. Understanding how R handles memory, and when it makes copies of objects, helps us avoid these.

    How R handles memory

    When you run x <- c(1, 2, 3), R does two things. It creates a vector in memory, and it binds the name x to that vector. The name is a reference to the object, not the object itself. So y <- x doesn’t copy anything: x and y both point to the same object.

    R makes a copy only when you modify an object that has more than one name. This is called copy-on-modify. You can watch it happen with tracemem(), which prints a message every time an object is copied:

    R 

    x <- c(1, 2, 3)
tracemem(x)
y <- x          # no copy: two names, one object
y[[3]] <- 4     # copy: changing y must not change x
#> tracemem[0x55d5c8e0b2a8 -> 0x55d5c8e0b6f8]:
y[[2]] <- 10    # no copy: y now has its own object, with one name
untracemem(x)

    If only one name points to an object, R can usually modify it in place without copying – that’s what’s happening in the last line.

    This has some practical consequences:

    • Passing an object to a function does not copy it. R copies the object only if the function modifies it.
    • Every copy takes time and memory. A copy inside a loop is made on every iteration, so loops are where copies cost the most.
    • Memory used by an object is freed automatically once no name points to it. R’s garbage collector does this in the background, so you rarely need to call gc() yourself.
    Callout

    RStudio’s Environment pane holds its own references to objects. This can make tracemem() report copies you wouldn’t see if you ran R in a terminal or rendered an R Markdown/Quarto document.

    Avoid creating unnecessary objects

    Here are some tips to avoid creating objects unnecessarily:

    • Re-use temporary variable names, e.g. x <- x + 1 instead of y <- x + 1. The old value of x then has no name pointing to it, so its memory can be freed.
    • Don’t save intermediate results unnecessarily; compute them on the fly.
    • Use rm() to remove large objects when they are no longer needed. This removes the name, so the garbage collector can free the memory.
    • Cache variables: calculate an object once and reuse the value when necessary. For example, if sd(x) appears in several function calls, define sd_x <- sd(x) once and reuse it.

    Data structures

    Use the simplest data structure that does the job. This minimises the amount of memory you need and the work R has to do. For example:

    • If you have rectangular data of the same type, prefer a matrix to a data frame.
    • Use logical or integer vectors instead of numeric (double) vectors where possible. They need 4 bytes per element instead of 8.
    • Use unnamed objects instead of named objects.

    It is especially important to use low-level structures for computation. You can create richer objects as a final step before returning them to the user.

    Callout

    Data frames are lists of columns. Modifying one column copies only that column, but modifying a row copies every column. If you need to update data row by row in a loop, work on a matrix or on separate vectors instead, and build the data frame at the end.

    Don’t grow objects

    In R, growing objects with a loop is notoriously slow. When you use c(), append(), cbind(), rbind() or paste() to make an object bigger, R can’t extend the existing object in place. It must allocate space for a new object and copy the old one into it. Repeating this on every iteration means copying more and more data each time, so the total work grows with the square of the final length.

    Let’s compare three ways of creating a sequence of numbers. We will wrap each one in a function, to make it easier to benchmark their performance.

    Method 1: grow the object

    R 

    grow <- function(n) {
   vec <- numeric(0)
   for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      vec <- c(vec, i)
   }
   vec
}

    Method 2: create an object of the final length, then change its values by subsetting:

    R 

    pre_allocate <- function(n) {
   vec <- numeric(n)
   for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      vec[i] <- i
   }
   vec
}
    Callout

    numeric(n), integer(n), logical(n) and character(n) initialise vectors of length n of the type given as the function name. To initialise a list, we can use vector(mode = "list", length = n).

    Method 3: create the final object directly

    R 

    direct <- function(n) {
   seq_len(n)
}
    Callout

    Note that many sequences can be created directly with seq() and rep(). See their help pages to learn about all their arguments.

    Challenge

    Challenge

    Which of grow(), pre_allocate() and direct() do you expect to perform best and why? Which of the methods do you think will scale best as n increases? Which do you think will scale worst?

    Use microbenchmarking to test your intuition. Try different values of n. At what size do you start to notice differences?

    In which method do you get to the underlying C code the fastest?

    Which method(s) create copies? In which method(s) are objects modified in place?

    R 

    n <- 10000
bench::mark(
   grow(n),
   pre_allocate(n),
   direct(n)
)

    WARNING 

    Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
disabled.

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 3 × 6
  expression           min   median  `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr>      <bch:tm> <bch:tm>      <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 grow(n)            102ms    107ms       9.25     382MB    96.2
2 pre_allocate(n)    407µs    413µs    2346.      98.6KB     4.00
3 direct(n)          450ns    591ns 1207034.          0B     0

    Note the orders of magnitude difference in the results. pre_allocate(10000) is over 300 times faster than grow(10000). Where it is possible to directly specify your vector, that is orders of magnitude faster again. In this case, direct(10000) is nearly 1500 times faster than pre_allocate(10000). That’s quite the speed-up!

    Look at the mem_alloc column too. grow() allocates far more memory than the size of its final result, because it makes a new copy on every iteration.

    When n <- 10000000, method 1 takes about an hour, whereas method 3 is pretty much instantaneous.

    Challenge

    Monopoly revisted

    In profiling with profvis, there was a challenge to profile the simulate_monopoly() function from the efficient package. You should have identified that most of the time is spent in the function move_square().

    1. Use View(move_square) to view the source code. Copy the code to a new .R file and rename the function move_square2. Edit move_square2() to speed up the slow parts of the code, taking into account the optimisations discussed in this episode and the previous one on base R optimisations.
    2. Create a wrapper to run a specified move square function n times with different seeds:

    R 

    run <- function(n, fun){
  x <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    set.seed(i)
    x[i] <- fun(1)
  }
  x
}
    1. Run bench::mark(run(n, move_square), run(n, move_square2)) with n = 1000 to test your changes.
    2. Finally, compare profvis(run(n, move_square)) with profvis(run(n, move_square2)).
    • What is the simplest data structure that could be used to store the roles of the dice?
    • Are there faster built-in functions that could be used?
    • Consider the logical operations

    R 

    move_square2 <- function(current) {
  # data.frame -> matrix
  rolls = matrix(sample(1:6, 6, replace = TRUE), ncol = 2)
  Total = rowSums(rolls) # rowSums instead of apply      
  IsDouble = rolls[,1] == rolls[,2]
  # && instead of &
  if(IsDouble[1] && IsDouble[2] && IsDouble[3]) { 
    current = 11#Go To Jail
  } else if(IsDouble[1] && IsDouble[2]) {
    current = current + sum(Total[1:3])
  } else if(IsDouble[1]) {
    current = current + sum(Total[1:2])
  } else {
    current = current + Total[1]
  }
  current ## don't need return()
}

n <- 1000
bench::mark(run(n, efficient::move_square), run(n, move_square2))

    WARNING 

    Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is
disabled.

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 2 × 6
  expression                          min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr>                     <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 run(n, efficient::move_square)  224.9ms    227ms      4.40    6.06MB     32.3
2 run(n, move_square2)             12.5ms   17.3ms     61.7   150.14KB     36.6
    Key Points
    • Names point to objects in memory. R copies an object only when you modify one that has more than one name (copy-on-modify).
    • Use tracemem() to see when R copies an object.
    • Avoid creating objects unnecessarily.
    • Use the simplest data structure for your needs.
    • Do not grow objects. Create them directly if you can. Otherwise, pre-allocate the memory before running a loop.
